reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The syndrome reflects functional or anatomical hemisection of the spinal cord, producing a characteristic laterally split, dissociated deficit
Below the lesion there is ipsilateral weakness from corticospinal tract damage and ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration and fine touch from dorsal column involvement

On the opposite side there is loss of pain and temperature sensation, beginning one or two segments below the level of the lesion, because spinothalamic fibres decussate shortly after entering the cord
At the level of the lesion there may be ipsilateral segmental lower motor neurone signs and a narrow band of ipsilateral sensory loss
The pure anatomical form is uncommon, and most patients present with an incomplete Brown-Sequard-plus picture
Penetrating trauma such as a stab wound is a classic cause, but tumour, prolapsed disc, epidural haematoma, demyelination and radiation myelopathy are all recognised
The offset between the higher motor and dorsal column level and the lower contralateral pain and temperature level is a useful clue to true lesion height
MRI of the cord with contrast is the key investigation and helps identify a treatable structural cause
reference.pathophysiology: Brown-Sequard syndrome results from injury to one lateral half of the spinal cord, which interrupts three long tracts with differing decussation patterns. The corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so its interruption causes weakness on the same side as the cord lesion; the dorsal columns ascend uncrossed to the lower medulla, so their damage causes ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration; the spinothalamic tract, by contrast, decussates within one or two segments of entering the cord, so its interruption causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning just below the lesion. This anatomy explains the distinctive dissociated and laterally divided pattern of deficit and the slight vertical offset between the sensory modalities.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spinal cord with contrast to localise and characterise the causative lesion
CT of the spine where bony injury or instability from trauma is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and oligoclonal bands if a demyelinating cause is considered
Serum aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies where inflammatory myelopathy is possible
Coagulation studies where a spontaneous epidural haematoma is suspected
Careful examination for a penetrating wound tract in trauma
redFlags: Progressive deficit suggesting an expanding compressive lesion or haematoma
Traumatic injury with spinal instability requiring immobilisation
New sphincter dysfunction indicating more extensive cord involvement
An ascending sensory or motor level over hours
reference.prognosis: Brown-Sequard syndrome carries the most favourable prognosis of the incomplete cord syndromes, and the majority of patients regain the ability to walk and achieve useful bladder control. Outcome is best when a treatable cause is addressed promptly before secondary cord injury accrues.
pitfalls: Expecting sensory loss on the same side as the weakness and forgetting that spinothalamic loss is contralateral
Missing a subtle contralateral pinprick deficit and thereby overlooking the diagnosis
Assuming the syndrome only follows penetrating trauma and neglecting compressive or inflammatory causes
Mislocating the lesion by relying on the lower contralateral pain and temperature level rather than the higher ipsilateral signs
Failing to image urgently when a compressive cause is potentially reversible
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat the underlying cause promptly with surgical decompression and stabilisation for penetrating trauma, tumour, prolapsed disc, or epidural haematoma before secondary cord injury accrues
Deliver acute spinal cord injury care with immobilisation, maintenance of cord perfusion, and urgent neurosurgical referral
Give disease-specific therapy for inflammatory causes, such as corticosteroids for demyelinating or inflammatory myelopathy
Institute early physiotherapy and occupational therapy rehabilitation to maximise motor recovery and gait
Manage bladder and bowel dysfunction with intermittent catheterisation and a bowel regimen, and treat neuropathic pain
Prevent complications with venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, pressure-area care, and spasticity management within a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team
